articles.title: Woman doesn’t reply to colleague on social media—days later, she’s let go
articles.summary: Fired for being "unprofessional" online, TikTok creator Charlotte Blandford Tagg says many share her confusion.
articles.body:
A content creator who says she was fired from her job for being "unprofessional online" has told Newsweek she believes her experience is becoming increasingly common, as more employees find their off-the-clock social media presence colliding with their employer's expectations.

Charlotte Blandford Tagg, who has amassed more than 46,000 followers on TikTok , was let go from her position at a small magazine on August 27, after failing her probationary period. The reason given, she said, was straightforward. Former bosses told her she had been "unprofessional online."

"I was working as a content creator for the magazine, and I've been creating content and posting online for around four years," Blandford Tagg, from England, told Newsweek . "I was specifically dismissed for failing my probation, with the reason given being that I had been 'unprofessional online.'"

Her case has sparked upset among her followers, resonating with a wider swath of the workforce navigating the blurred line between personal expression and professional obligation.

"I think this is becoming increasingly common because people want—and often need—to earn more money than their wages allow," she said. "Single mothers in particular have huge pressures on them, and those pressures are only increasing."

Blandford Tagg's TikTok bio declares that she "likes to overshare," though her content is largely in line with the confessional, slice-of-life style that has become ubiquitous on such platforms.

Her most viral video , posted May 13, has racked up more than 1.3 million views. In it, she speaks candidly about an incident of racism connected to her son's primary school, describing how she plans to teach him that people of all ethnic backgrounds deserve equal treatment, in hopes his outlook might ripple outward to other children.

The comments section is overwhelmingly supportive, with viewers on TikTok praising her openness.

Still, Blandford Tagg acknowledged that her public account—and the attention it draws—has, at times, created friction. She said the situation leading up to her redundancy was compounded when someone who had been lined up to work for the company for free complained to her manager that Blandford Tagg had failed to respond to them, while apparently still finding time to post TikToks.

"I don't think people should have to give up their lives outside of work simply because they have a job," she said. "People should be allowed to do what they want outside of their 9–5."

The backlash to her firing, she said, reflects how deeply social media is now woven into everyday life.

"It's fun, it's community, it's a source of income and, in a world where we're constantly getting glimpses into other people's homes and minds, I think we should be entering an era where the person you are at work and the person you are online can be different," she said, adding: "However, I did work for a small-town, small-minded company, so perhaps it shouldn't have come as a huge surprise!

Blandford Tagg kept the name of her former employer private and has since joined No Shame, a PR agency start-up geared toward women who do not necessarily fit conventional notions of professionalism.

"I think the word 'professional' has sometimes become another word for 'robot,'" she said. "I don't think you should have to hide your personality or your life to be taken seriously at work."

Her situation is playing out against a backdrop of staggering platform reach. TikTok counts roughly 26.8 million users in the U.K., where Blandford Tagg is based, and 1.99 billion monthly active users worldwide, according to software company Sprout Social, while DemandSage puts the worldwide figure at 2.21 billion.

Newsweek spoke to several career experts about why conflicts like Blandford Tagg's appear to be multiplying.

Sam Wright, head of career strategy at Huntr.co, framed it as a question of control.

"Many businesses see the strong social following of an employee as an asset in today's age where attention is difficult to come by but they want it on their terms," Wright said, predicting that as audiences become currency, "more and more employees will be expected to have an audience… and this issue of who controls social media will grow."

Lacey Kaelani, CEO of job search engine Metaintro, argued that the content itself often matters less than its traceability.

"A joke told to a friend is perfectly fine whereas a joke on camera is a problem," she said, describing employees with large followings as "a channel that the company can associate themselves with but has absolutely no control of."

She likened firms' attempts to police off-hours behavior to the erosion of non-compete clauses, adding that fired workers "can now reach audiences much broader than previously" by explaining why they lost their jobs .

Career strategist Michelle Enjoli said the underlying issue is one of blurred identity.

"Your online presence has become an extension of your professional reputation," she said.

Her proposed fix? Clearer, written boundaries.

"The solution is a clearer conversation that defines what's off-limits versus what's just personality," she said.

Blandford Tagg's former employer could not be reached for comment because she chose to keep their identity private.

Update 9/8/26, 11:54 a.m. ET: This article was updated with additional information.

Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Charlotte Nisbet and Emma Lee-Sang

articles.title: Newlywed finds out husband okayed his entire family staying 5-6 weeks in their small 2-bedroom apartment,  leaving her ready to flee to her parents
articles.summary: A freshly married couple still figuring out how to share a closet. Tiny two-bedroom apartment in furnace weather. Then a full guest list sneaks in through th...
articles.body:
A newly married couple finds themselves hosting the husband's extended family for an unexpected 5-6 week stay in their small two-bedroom apartment without prior consent.

The wife is faced with the challenge of accommodating her in-laws' strict vegetarian lifestyle and moral standards, conflicting with her own habits and beliefs in her own home.

Despite promises of respecting boundaries and partnership, the husband's lack of support and the imposition of his family's extended stay raises questions about consent and autonomy within the marriage.

A freshly married couple still figuring out how to share a closet. Tiny two-bedroom apartment in furnace weather. Then a full guest list sneaks in through the group chat. Parents-in-law, sister-in-law, her husband, and a kid. Five to six weeks. Not a long weekend not a quick visit. An entire season of television, but in real life and with zero writers

This story makes me think marriage really should come with brochures like the ones nursing homes or private schools used to have, only with an extra section titled surprise extended family residency not included, but absolutely will happen

WIBTAH if I went to stay with my parents for a couple of weeks because my husband's family planned a 5-6 week stay in our 2BHK without asking me?

This story is great and infuriating in many ways, but what I find the "funniest" is the way consent gets retrofitted after the fact. Tickets are booked, dates decided, sleeping arrangements implied, and only then does anyone casually drop how long they are staying. Apparently, the new household policy is inform not ask. Somewhere in there the phrase our home quietly shifts into his family's base camp.

Add in the lifestyle remix. The in-laws are strict vegetarians with bonus moral authority. No eggs in the house. Meanwhile, the actual residents live on non-veg and thought their kitchen was theirs. Six weeks of performing someone else's diet, dress code, and behavioral standards in what is supposed to be the safest room on the map. That is less hospitality and more low-budget re-education retreat.

Her family and friends are on the opposite side of the country. This apartment is not just a home. It is the entire social universe. Turning it into a six-week hostel run by his relatives is not a small inconvenience. It is a full-scale occupation of the only space that actually belongs to her.

For years, he sells the dream. He gets it. He respects space. He will run interference. This is the non-negotiable boundary. Then the moment arrives and the response is a shrug dressed up as diplomacy. What can he do? Everything is already booked. As if airline confirmation emails have more authority than his spouse.

The tension is not about being anti-family. It is about watching every promise of partnership fold the second his side wants something. Boundaries were discussed in theory. Now the experiment is live, and suddenly she is the only person expected to adjust.

images.caption: I (29F) got married in December (less than 3 months as of today) after being with my husband (29M) for almost 7 years.
One thing I've always been very clear about with him, both before and after marriage, is that I need my space and that decisions about people staying in our home should involve both of us.
Recently I found out that his sister, her husband, their child, and my in- laws have all booked tickets to come stay with us.
That's about 5-6 weeks. I would be more than happy to host them for 1-2 weeks but 5-6 weeks seems too overwhelming at this stage.
The part that really upset me is that no one asked me beforehand. I only found out after everything was already booked.
Stressed woman sitting on a couch with her hand on her forehead while a man sits in the background facing away after an argument.
That too when it was asked that how long they were planning to stay. We live in a 2- bedroom apartment in is an extremely hot climate, and this will mean 7 people total in the house in peak summer.
My husband will be at work most of the day, so I'll be the one at home with everyone.

articles.title: Former Connecticut official convicted of bribery asks judge to spare him prison
articles.summary: Konstantimos "Kosta" Diamantis, who is facing up to 13 years in prison for bribery, asked a judge to consider home detention instead.
articles.body:
Konstantimos "Kosta" Diamantis, a former state school construction official convicted of taking bribes, is asking a federal court for home detention and maximum probation instead of up to 13 years as prison sentencing guidelines recommend.

"Mr. Diamantis does not minimize the seriousness of the jury's verdict or his breach of the public trust," his attorney, Norm Pattis, wrote in a motion to the U.S. Judge Stefon Underhill at U.S. District Court in Bridgeport.

Diamantis is scheduled to be sentenced Sept. 17 after a jury last October found him guilty of 21 counts of bribery, extortion, conspiracy and making false statements to federal investigators.

He has been free on a $500,000 bond since his arrest several years ago and was allowed to remain on bond after his conviction.

The prosecution argued Diamantis used his position as head of the state's Office of School Construction Grants and Review to steer contracts on school projects in exchange for more than $75,000 in bribes.

In his motion, Pattis urged the court to consider all the circumstances surrounding Diamantis' crimes and the current situation of his 70-year-old client.

"He asks the Court to impose an individualized sentence based on all the circumstances rather than treating the advisory range as presumptively appropriate," Pattis said.

That sentence, Pattis continued, would not include jail time but would contain strict restrictions against future government employment or contracting, financial disclosure and monitoring, payment of restitution when appropriate and a prohibition against profiting from his crimes.

"His request rests on the combined force of his age, lack of physical dangerousness, loss of the position that enabled the conduct, financial ruin, loss of professional status, diminished earning capacity, family circumstances, and the limited additional sentencing value of a decade or more in prison," Pattis said.

Diamantis also faces a second trial, his state pension is likely to be forfeited, his $2,600 a month in social security would cease if incarcerated and future employment prospects are slight, Pattis added.

A second trial is scheduled for early next year for additional public corruption charges. Federal prosecutors claim Diamantis, who has forfeited his law license and is a former state lawmaker, quashed a state audit of an eye care practice that was engaged in healthcare fraud when he was employed in the governor's budget department, the Office of Policy and Management.

articles.title: He Bought a $3,000 Sony TV. When It Broke, Sony Threatened Him With a $500K Lawsuit
articles.summary: Sony India threatened a customer with a 5 crore rupee lawsuit after he built a website documenting his denied Bravia TV warranty claim.
articles.body:
A customer purchased a Sony Bravia TV under warranty, but when vertical green lines appeared on the screen, Sony classified it as "external damage" and demanded $307 for repair instead of honoring the warranty.

Sony responded to the customer's public criticism by sending a legal notice threatening $500K in damages if the customer did not take down a website documenting the warranty dispute.

Legal commentary suggests Sony's actions resemble strategic legal pressure to silence critics rather than resolve disputes, raising concerns about the risks of publicly criticizing corporations.

Spend $3,000 on a premium TV. Twenty-two months later, vertical green lines crawl across the screen. You're still under warranty. Sony sends a technician . The technician says: external damage. No free repair. That'll be $307, please. You document everything and build a website. Sony responds with a six-page legal notice threatening $500K in damages. This is not a hypothetical. This happened — and it raises an uncomfortable question about how much risk comes with criticizing a corporation publicly when you may already be paying too much for the privilege.

When "External Damage" Means Whatever Sony Needs It to Mean

The facts here are straightforward, which is precisely what makes them worse.

In September 2024 , a customer purchased a 55-inch Sony Bravia Mini LED TV for ₹150,031, covered by a three-year Sony warranty and a two-year extended warranty from retailer Croma, according to Navbharat Times.

Vertical green lines appeared around 22 months into ownership — well inside the warranty window.

Sony's technician classified the defect as "external damage" despite no visible dent or crack, and never provided the detailed technical report the customer repeatedly requested, per Navbharat Times.

Sony quoted ₹29,130 ($307) for panel replacement instead of honoring the warranty. Sportskeeda Tech reports the technician admitted on video that he never physically inspected the internal panel and lacked engineering qualifications.

A diagnosis made from photos, without opening the device, by someone without engineering credentials is not a diagnosis. It is a liability shield dressed up as a verdict. Worth noting: Sony has historically run free evaluation and repair programs for specific Bravia models when systemic issues emerge, per Sony's own support documentation. That generosity, apparently, has limits — not unlike the pattern seen when dealers keep recommending a $300 fix consumers never actually needed.

"The notice referenced damages of up to ₹5 crore if he did not comply." — according to Sportskeeda Tech

A $500K Crore Threat Is Not Customer Service

Sony's legal escalation arrived before its warranty dispute was ever resolved.

The customer did what anyone does in the era of viral Reddit threads and public callout posts — he documented everything. He registered SonyBravia.com, launched a site called " Sorry Bravia ," and published a full chronological timeline, photographs, and service communications. He posted "Never buy a Sony Bravia." Sony's response on September 1, 2026: a six-page legal notice demanding the site come down, the domain be surrendered, and an unconditional apology be issued — or face civil and criminal defamation proceedings, per Entertales.

Legal commentary cited by Legal Suvidha describes Sony's move as resembling SLAPP tactics — strategic legal pressure designed to silence critics rather than resolve disputes. Sony's notice reportedly argues the SonyBravia.com domain misuses its trademark and could mislead consumers into thinking they have reached an official brand page. That is a recognizable legal concern. It collapses fast, though, when Sony had not resolved a warranty claim on a ₹1.5 lakh TV before reaching for a ₹5 crore in damages legal weapon.

The customer has refused to remove the site. His consumer complaint remains pending in India's court system. The case is unresolved — and any consumer who has ever left a one-star review online may want to pay attention to how it ends, particularly anyone who has already wrestled with frustrating computer problems and the indifferent support that often follows.

articles.title: 11 European nations and Canada announce trade sanctions on Israeli settlements in the West Bank
articles.summary: British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband accused "settler terrorists" of "ethnic cleansing" in areas of the West Bank and said the UK was bringing in an "import...
articles.body:
The UK and France were among 12 countries to announce new trade sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank on Tuesday, amid what they called a "rapidly deteriorating" situation marked by increasing settler attacks on Palestinians.

Canada, Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain, and Sweden joined the UK and France in confirming plans to introduce restrictions on trade with settlements, according to a joint statement from the countries' foreign ministers.

"The Government of Israel's actions in the West Bank are undermining the possibility of a two-State solution," the statement reads, adding that there have been "unprecedented levels of settler violence and settlement expansion."

"Together, we are resolute: the two-state solution must be protected, and we will take action in pursuit of a just and lasting peace," it continued.

It comes after the Israeli government last month opened up tenders for the construction of around 1,200 housing units in the West Bank, drawing widespread condemnation from the international community and human rights groups.

The units, destined for the E1 settlement area, would further isolate East Jerusalem from the rest of the territory.

In their statement on Tuesday, the 12 foreign ministers called the decision to publish tenders "unacceptable."

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, French President Emmanuel Macron and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney "have agreed on the need to take action to prevent further damage," the statement added.

Speaking to parliament on Tuesday, British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband accused "settler terrorists" of "ethnic cleansing" in areas of the West Bank, saying that the Israeli government had often "turned a blind eye to this."

He announced that the UK would also be bringing in an "import ban on goods from illegal settlements in the occupied territories."

"I do not believe the British people want us supporting the occupation by accepting products from settlements in our shops and supermarkets," he told MPs.

In a post on X, Miliband's French counterpart, Jean-Noël Barrot, said Paris had taken the decision to enforce the sanctions as the West Bank was "on the brink of explosion."

"Unchecked expansion of settlements in violation of international law, a surge in violence committed by extremist settlers against Palestinians, and acts of terror condemned by the Israeli authorities themselves," he wrote.

Burnham later issued his own statement on Tuesday evening, calling the newly announced measures "carefully judged, targeted steps that are not aimed at the Israeli people, but at the unacceptable policies of the current Israeli government."

"Before I became Prime Minister, I said our country's response had been too slow and simply not good enough. That's why I committed to changing the government's approach," the UK leader added.

Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar on Tuesday ordered the closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem in response to the moves taken by Westminster, as he hit out at Miliband's statement.

"The accusations made today by the foreign secretary in the British Parliament were outrageous lies," Sa'ar said.

Israel has also announced that it will henceforth refuse entry to 12 British nationals.

The list reportedly includes former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn, his Your Party cofounder and MP for Coventry South Zarah Sultana, and Diane Abbott, the MP for Hackney North and Stoke Newington.

The West Bank has been occupied by Israel since 1967 and has seen a surge in violence since the start of the war in Gaza, which broke out following the Hamas militant group's attacks on Israel on 7 October 2023.

According to a report from the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, there were around 737,000 Israeli settlers in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, as of October 2024.

Israeli settlements in the West Bank are illegal under international law.

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy juror admitted 'reasonable doubt' but still refused insanity verdict, foreperson says
articles.summary: Three Lindsay Clancy jurors say a lone holdout admitted having reasonable doubt but still refused to deliver a not guilty by insanity verdict.
articles.body: Three people who served on the jury in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial are speaking publicly for the first time after last week's mistrial, saying a lone holdout prevented the panel from reaching a unanimous verdict. The jurors, including the foreperson, said one juror acknowledged having reasonable doubt but still refused to find Clancy not guilty by reason of insanity, according to interviews with NBC10 Boston. The jurors' accounts offer the first public glimpse inside the deliberations that ended in a deadlocked jury. The mistrial came after days of deliberations in the closely watched case against Clancy, the Massachusetts mother accused of killing her three young children in January 2023. "He admitted he had reasonable doubt and I started filling out the forms, I was so excited," the foreperson told NBC10 Boston. LINDSAY CLANCY JUDGE CALLS MISTRIAL, THEN GRANTS DEFENSE ONE HOUR STAY FOR APPEAL But the foreperson said the juror then added, "But I'm still not going to say that she's not guilty by reason of insanity." The foreperson said she had already begun completing the verdict paperwork after believing the jury had reached an agreement. "There were three forms I had to fill out, and I started filling them out. I wrote my signature on each one," she told the station. "But then he said, 'But I'm still not going to say she's not guilty by reason of insanity.'" LINDSAY CLANCY ATTORNEY KEVIN REDDINGTON SIGNALS HE'S OPEN TO A DEAL, HOPES DA WILL 'REVISIT' CASE Clancy admitted to the killings but pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity, arguing she was suffering from severe mental illness at the time. Prosecutors maintained she was criminally responsible for the deaths. The foreperson also told the station she wrote the note to the judge raising concerns that one juror had expressed reasonable doubt but would not agree to a verdict. The three jurors said they became frustrated with the holdout during deliberations, claiming he refused to consider the views of the rest of the panel. "He was very arrogant. He really did not take anything that anybody said," one juror told NBC10 Boston. The juror said the holdout questioned evidence about Clancy's medications even after the panel reviewed toxicology reports from South Shore Hospital that had been admitted into evidence. MOM ‘VERY INVESTED’ IN LINDSAY CLANCY CASE HIRES CASEY ANTHONY ATTORNEY AFTER ALLEGEDLY KILLING SON: DOCS "There were nurses on the jury. Yes, they spoke to that specific thing," the juror said. "That was a question that he had, and he just completely disregarded the information that they gave him." "Every one of us in the hours of our frustration would get up and walk the room because you just couldn't sit anymore," another juror told the station. "He would not interact with us and try to understand." The juror said the panel repeatedly read the judge's instructions on reasonable doubt to the holdout. "We read to him, on numerous occasions, the definition of reasonable doubt from Judge Sullivan's instruction," she said. The same juror said the holdout "had the hardest time getting over the fact that Lindsay viciously killed her children," despite the panel's discussions about whether Clancy met the legal standard for insanity. NBC10 Boston reported it attempted to contact the juror identified by the others as the holdout but had not received a response. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP A judge declared a mistrial last week after jurors informed the court they were hopelessly deadlocked following several days of deliberations. It remains unclear whether prosecutors will seek to retry the case.

articles.title: Should promotion depend on how workers use AI?
articles.summary: More companies are tying career progression to AI use: is that fair?
articles.body:
It's in Duncan Trevithick's interest to be good at using AI at work - if he can use it to get more tasks done, faster, he'll qualify for a bonus at the end of the year.

On the surface, it's a great incentive. But he's questioning what's really in it for him.

"The uncomfortable interpretation is that employees are being assessed on how effectively they can participate in their own redundancy," says Spain-based Trevithick, 34, who works in marketing for an AI training data company.

But if he uses AI to take care of two days worth of work each week, he says the financial rewards don't add up.

"I do not receive two days off or a 40% pay rise. The higher output simply becomes the new baseline. In the short term, that may help me get promoted. In the longer term, I have helped prove how much of my job no longer requires me," he says.

"I'm just trying to view myself as a manager, and I'm managing some people, and I'm also managing AI agents, or AI loops, or whatever you want to call it."

Using employees' AI abilities as a measure of whether they should get a bonus, promoted - or even sacked - is fast becoming more common.

Accenture CEO Julie Sweet told the Rapid Response podcast in March: "Today, AI at Accenture is how we do work. So if you want to get promoted, you've got to do the things that we do in order to operate at Accenture."

And big names like Disney, Meta, JP Morgan and KPMG have introduced "AI leaderboards" to track and rank employees' usage of the array of LLMs and platforms at their disposal, according to media reports . Crypto trading platform Coinbase has already fired engineers who didn't complete AI training, as requested by the chief executive, Brian Armstrong .

It demonstrates how eager business leaders are to see a return from their AI investments, especially when 94% of companies have yet to see significant value from AI, according to a report by consultants McKinsey.

Employees feel they have to get on board, thanks to the current state of the jobs market - in the UK, vacancies have hit a five-year low .

Meanwhile, 75% of the 1,881 UK jobseekers polled in July by recruiter Gi Group say they would not be put off applying to an organisation that had introduced AI proficiency into individual performance reviews. Around 22% said it would be off-putting.

"It's like being in the sea and you see a giant wave coming. You can get out a surfboard and try and ride it as long as possible, or you can just let it take you under. But you can't stop the wave," says Trevithick.

But what's going on at the large consultancy Pamela (her name has been changed to protect her identity) works for isn't sitting right with her.

She's a US-based senior executive who has observed that, while there isn't a formal mandate for employees to use AI, it's obviously determining who is rewarded, and who is left behind.

"The ground is shifting under us. You've got to demonstrate [AI] fluency and fluidity as one of your key achievements. It's kind of quiet where nobody's saying, 'learn AI or else'. But let me tell you, in performance reviews, they reward who uses it well," says Pamela.

That shift, she adds, means that AI capabilities are now counting for more than actual experience, which is creating a "two tier workforce".

"You've got the same job title, same tenure, but different value based on whether someone treats AI as a threat or a tool - that gap widens really quickly once leadership notices it," says Pamela.

"AI fluency beats credentials every day. Somebody that has 15, 20 years of experience and no AI fluency will be passed over for those that have, say, three years, but are fast with the tools."

She adds: "If you're not visibly using AI, you see slower promotion timelines. It's harder to be seen, and it's harder to fight being on that shortlist."

But is it legal for companies to shift the goal posts like this?

Legally, bosses are in the clear, confirms Tina Chander, partner and employment lawyer at Weightmans. But she says it does open up questions about pay and fairness.

"The question then becomes whether the employer increases expectations on the basis that the employee can now produce more work. Is that fair?" questions Chander.

"And if an employee is effectively doing more because AI has made them more efficient, should they be rewarded differently? Or are they effectively making themselves redundant, thus acting as a disincentive to be productive?"

Chander advises businesses to have clear policies, training and boundaries in place, otherwise they risk employees opening up disputes about fairness, performance expectations and job security.

Indeed, from January 2027, UK employees will have six months to submit unfair dismissal claims compared with the current three months, and will be able to do so after just six months service , rather than the current two years.

Yet HR consultant Tina Rahman says employers aren't currently being transparent enough in telling employees why they want AI to be part of people's jobs, and what the end purpose of that is - which she agrees is to save costs and time, but also to cut down on outsourcing.

"Because they misunderstand it, this is not being reflected to employees," says Rahman, who runs a London-based consultancy, HR Habitat.

A lack of clarity around AI usage is certainly causing discontent at Pamela's company.

"Leadership is being inconsistent and vague on purpose. Firms want productivity gains without owning the disruption narrative," she says.

"If something goes wrong, they're going to say, 'I didn't tell you to do that. Where'd you get that from?' Then if you did something with AI, and it works, great."

Mandating AI use at work can become purely performative, rather than having any real positive impact, warns Kamila Miller, applied AI researcher and lecturer at Henley Business School.

"Make AI usage a KPI [key performance indicator], and people will log their interactions to hit the metric, route work through a chatbot that did not need it, and generate AI-flavoured outputs that look productive on a dashboard. You will measure adoption. You will not measure judgement, learning, or better decisions," states Miller, who is based in Reading.

"You have not made people more skilled - you have made them more obedient."

Some firms have acknowledged those arguments.

In April, Luis von Ahn, the CEO of Duolingo, told the podcast Silicon Valley Girl that his language learning firm is no longer using AI use as part of performance reviews.

"We found that people... were asking: 'Do you want us to use AI for AI's sake?'

"In the end we backtracked and we said: 'Look, the most important thing for your performance is that you are doing, whatever your job is, as well as possible. A lot of times AI can help you with that. But if it can't, I'm not going to force you to do that.'"

Meanwhile, in May, the Financial Times reported that Amazon had shut down an internal leaderboard which tracked employee's use of AI. The report said employees had been attempting to climb the rankings by setting AI needless tasks.

Despite those high-profile moves, some staff still they need to show AI proficiency - Pamela is one of those.

In her mid 50s, she plans to retire within 10 years, and wants to keep her job so she doesn't risk losing any pension and health benefits. She's visibly stepping up how AI is helping her bring in new clients, and making sure she's being credited for it.

As for Duncan Trevithick, he's doing his best to future proof himself with a number of side projects.

"If AI can do a job better than you can, it makes sense for the business to replace you. That's how the capitalist model works. So it's about, how can you move into a position where you own assets where you can leverage AI, and then you benefit," says Trevithick.

articles.title: Meta continues to run ads promoting child sexual abuse material in India: report
articles.summary: The report follows a BBC Eye investigation that found Instagram running paid ads promoting such material in India.
articles.body:
Warning: This story contains descriptions of abuse

Meta ran hundreds of paid ads with artificial intelligence-generated child sexual abuse imagery, including several in India, over the past 10 months, a new report by US-based campaigners has found.

The report comes two months after the Indian government ordered Meta to remove all ads and content promoting child sexual abuse material (CSAM) on Instagram. This was in the aftermath of a BBC Eye investigation which found that Instagram was running paid adverts promoting CSAM in India.

Washington-based Tech Transparency Project (TTP) says it found 332 adverts with CSAM that ran on Facebook and Instagram, the majority of them (274) in August this year.

When the BBC wrote to Meta about these findings, they said in a statement, "We don't tolerate nudify apps or any kind of child exploitation, whether real or AI-generated. These criminals constantly shift tactics to evade detection, which is why we keep strengthening our detection and enforcement."

The TTP report, published on Tuesday, says that it identified several photos of real children, including a member of a European royal family, that were used in the ads and then manipulated using AI. It says more than a dozen ads appeared on Meta platforms even after TTP made the company aware of its findings.

About a quarter (84) of the ads ran in India and 78 of these were published after the Indian government's order on removing CSAM and its meeting with senior Meta officials.

After the BBC investigation, several Indian agencies including the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights and the National Human Rights Commission have said they are examining the matter.

The distribution of CSAM is a criminal offence in India, while Meta's policy states that ads must not contain content that sexually exploits or endangers children.

When the BBC contacted Meta about its investigation, it said that when it becomes aware of apparent child exploitation, it reports it to the US-based National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) in compliance with its legal obligations.

The NCMEC is the centralised global reporting system for the online sexual exploitation of children.

But Bhuwan Ribhu, the founder of Just Rights for Children, a network of more than 250 organisations working to prevent violence against children in India, says this is not enough.

Just Rights for Children has filed a petition in India's Supreme Court, citing the BBC's findings, and asked for directions to social media platforms for mandatory reporting and identification of those promoting child sexual abuse material

"Social media companies are clearly flouting Indian laws by not reporting child sexual abuse content to Indian law enforcement agencies as mandated by our child protection laws," said Ribhu.

The TTP, a research initiative of the non-profit Campaign for Accountability that seeks to hold large technology companies accountable, said it found 332 ads featuring CSAM on Instagram and Facebook running in the US, UK, EU, Australia and India. They say they have reported all the ads to NCMEC.

According to TTP, almost all the ads they found start with a photo of a child, and, as the video plays, the photo is manipulated by AI to show them engaging in a graphic sexual act.

TTP described one ad which ran in India as: A photo of a preteen girl animated so that she performs a graphic sex act, with a voiceover that says, "There are no restrictions. All the characters are real people and there are many options. This is the AI men actually use." The BBC has not seen this ad.

According to TTP, the ad was posted by more than 50 different handles in India over a fortnight in August this year.

In July, after BBC's investigation, Meta had put out a detailed post on its website about how it fights child exploitation on its apps.

"Anyone on our platforms can report ads if they believe they violate our policies," it said.

TTP said that it tried reporting ads via Meta's own reporting system and that of the 84 ads that ran in India, they were able to report 55. Meta only gives the option of reporting ads when they are live.

For 43 of these, TTP got a reply that said, "We've taken a look and found that this ad doesn't go against our Advertising Standards."

For 11 ads, they were told that the content had already been removed. They haven't received a response yet for one ad.

When the BBC reached out to Meta for a comment, they said, "we've built strong defenses, including systems that block violating ads as well as ongoing monitoring in case we initially miss something: that's why many of the ads flagged to us had already been removed, most had fewer than 200 impressions, and the total ad spend was under $5,000".

TTP said that when it reached out to Meta for a response, all the ads they reported were removed.

This was similar to what happened during the BBC's investigation. When the BBC used Meta's reporting system to report one of the ads featuring child sexual abuse to Instagram, the platform did not take it down.

Later, when the BBC asked Meta for comment, it said it had already disabled several adverts and suspended the accounts posting them. The company said it had removed additional ads, disabled more accounts and blocked URLs for other content that violated its policies in response to the BBC's findings.

TTP said that the vast majority of the 332 ads they found directed users to AI image or video generation apps, mostly from Chinese developers.

The report alleged that by advertising these apps using images of child sexual abuse, the implication is that they can be used for creating or viewing CSAM.

Meta has said it prohibits promotion of nudify apps, which use AI to create fake non-consensual nude or sexually explicit images.

One of India's top cyber police officers, Shikha Goel, who is director of the Cyber Security Bureau in the Indian state of Telangana, told the BBC that one of the biggest challenges with CSAM is "the ease with which users can move from one platform to another, making it harder to nab them".

"We are hopeful that the government will be addressing this in its latest interactions with social media intermediaries and direct them accordingly," she added.

The ads that BBC had found in its investigation also directed users to another app - the messaging app Telegram - where they could buy the material for as little as 99 rupees [$1.05; £0.80].

Telegram told the BBC at the time that the company uses both automated and human moderation to tackle CSAM, and that it has "virtually eliminated the public spread of CSAM" on its platform.

Ads on Meta's platforms are only published after first being approved by its moderation technology. Its review system relies primarily on automation and is designed to check images, video, text and audio, as well as who the ad is targeting and where links send them to.

After the BBC's investigation, Meta had said that "no system is perfect" and that "determined criminals continue to try to exploit our platform, including through our advertising systems".

But TTP found that several of the ads featuring child sexual abuse were placed by Meta's own ad agency partners in China.

These partners, known as "resellers", channel billions of dollars' worth of Chinese advertising onto Facebook and Instagram. The partners did not respond to TTP's questions.

TTP said that new ads have continued to appear even after they made Meta aware of their report's findings. They shared details of 17 ads including 11 that ran in India on 1-2 September.

articles.title: Chris Mason: Burnham looks to show he will go further than Starmer with West Bank sanctions
articles.summary: It is hoped that coordinated action minimises the blowback to any one country from Israel or America, our political editor writes.
articles.body:
There is little doubt that the UK's decision to ban imports from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank is another significant shift in Britain's posture in the Middle East.

The announcement from the Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband , with the Prime Minister Andy Burnham alongside him in the House of Commons, comes almost exactly a year after the UK formally recognised a Palestinian state . And it comes garnished with blunt language about Israel's conduct.

This latest announcement is both a logical extension of that decision of 12 months ago, senior figures argue, but also, in words and actions, an expression of Burnham's desire to go further than his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer was willing to.

It is, Miliband believes, a re-assertion of the logic of eventually arriving at a two-state solution – a viable Palestinian state alongside Israel.

The foreign secretary passionately argued that the UK did have agency and could act – and to do nothing would amount to failure. "A strategy of passivity in the face of what is happening is not a strategy," is how Miliband put it in an interview with Jewish News .

There is a pride among his team that after a diplomatic effort over the summer, there is a breadth to the coordinated international action on this, with 11 other countries, including France and Canada, sharing the same approach.

"We provided a convening and coordinating role in pulling this together," one source told me, "but we didn't have to convince others to do this. They were coming to the same view themselves, so we agreed we should all go out and say this at the same time."

The hope is that coordinated action increases the likelihood that the measures will have an impact and minimises the blowback to any one country from Israel or America.

UK officials had anticipated one likely reaction from Israel would be the enforced closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem, which has indeed happened.

And while there is a weary acknowledgement that no one can be certain what President Donald Trump might say next about anything ever, it is noted in Whitehall that the initial reaction of the US Secretary of State Marco Rubio was pretty understated.

As for the domestic political context, plenty in the Labour movement and the wider British left have long clamoured for this to happen.

Around 140 Labour MPs went public with this demand at the beginning of the summer, and Burnham was explicit in his criticism of his predecessor's approach to the Middle East, writing in July: "Labour's initial response to the treatment of Gaza caused huge hurt. We got it wrong and I am sorry about that."

In recent years Labour has haemorrhaged support in many communities with a significant Muslim population, and so for a new Labour prime minister seeking to lure as many on the left – and beyond – under Labour's umbrella, this diplomatic intervention makes sense.

But the reaction of the Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch, writing in the Jewish Chronicle , is a reminder of another challenge for Burnham, both political and societal.

"Once again, British Jews find themselves warning their own government that its relentless demonisation of the world's only Jewish state risks fanning the flames of antisemitism here at home," Badenoch said.

Later, the Chief Rabbi Sir Ephraim Mirvis said it was "truly a dark day for Britain's Jews".

Last October, as Mayor of Greater Manchester, Andy Burnham was the local figurehead during the grim reality of an attack at the Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation Synagogue in the city .

Miliband has sought to address concerns about what Badenoch calls "demonisation" by making his view clear that "holding British Jews responsible for the actions of the Israeli government is antisemitism, pure and simple".

But Labour figures are keenly aware that at points in the last decade, under the leadership of Jeremy Corbyn, the Labour Party's relationship with many British Jews was dire, a situation Starmer sought to rectify as a priority in the early years of his leadership.

In other words, the party's recent relations with many British Jews has been fragile for some time - and many in the community already felt vulnerable after last year's attack in Manchester, and the later arson attacks on Jewish community ambulances in north-west London in the spring.

Burnham has to manage that anxiety while making the case for the changing stance the government is announcing, in the weeks before he meets many of his international counterparts for the first time.

articles.title: N3on vs. Sneako explained as AI streamer controversy leads to accusations of betrayal, clout chasing and fake friendship
articles.summary: US Streamers News: The friendship between Kick streamers N3on and Sneako has taken an unexpected turn after a disagreement over artificial intelligence spilled into a ve.
articles.body: The friendship between Kick streamers N3on and Sneako has taken an unexpected turn after a disagreement over artificial intelligence spilled into a very public clash. What began with N3on unveiling an AI version of himself quickly became a debate about friendship, loyalty, money and the future of streaming. Their exchange has since grown sharper, with both creators taking direct shots at each other online.N3on and Sneako clash over the AI streamer controversyThe dispute began after N3on announced that an AI version of himself would continue streaming on Kick around the clock, even when he was asleep or away from the platform. He presented the experiment as a major step for online content creation and described himself as the “first AI streamer in the world.”The announcement drew plenty of criticism, and Sneako was among those who objected. Rather than keeping his concerns private, Sneako launched into a lengthy public criticism of N3on and questioned why the streamer needed another source of revenue.“Yeah, N3on, this **** is ***ing r***ded. Do you not make enough money from all the gambling deals you take already? It gets to a point. What is this for? Is it for clout? So that [people] go, 'Oh my God, he's the first AI streamer.' What, you're the first one to start the domino effect to ruin streaming and brain-rot the world even more?”For N3on, the bigger issue was not the criticism itself. It was where that criticism happened. The streamer argued that someone he considered a friend should have contacted him directly instead of turning the disagreement into public content.“Why would you say that about your friend and go on a rant for 45 minutes? Tell me this in private and move on, dumb****. He's the most [disloyal] guy I've ever seen in my life. Literally. It's cool that we've known Sneako is like that. This isn't anything new.”Their history made the argument more personal. The pair have collaborated before and share a connection through Kick and their faith, making the sudden public fallout stand out even more.Sneako and N3on trade personal insults onlineThe disagreement soon moved beyond the AI project. During a collaboration with The Orthodox Muslim, Sneako questioned whether N3on was viewed as a serious figure by his audience.“If we're being real, people don't consider you to be a man. So you could talk this way, and you seem like a dumb little kid. He's the same age as [The Orthodox Muslim]. You don't speak to men like this. You get away with it because, deep down, you know people don't take you seriously. You're just a yapping little boy.”N3on responded by accusing Sneako of chasing attention at the expense of their friendship.“Sneako, **** yourself. You're a piece of ****. You'll do anything for views. You'll use religion for views. If you cared about me, you would text me, you would call me, you would talk to me, not make it public.”N3on later made his position even clearer, saying he had no issue with the AI concept itself. His frustration was with Sneako's decision to attack him publicly.“It was cool and interesting. **** off, **** Sneako... No matter what you think about your friends, if they're truly your friends and you value and care for them, then no matter what it is, you would never bash them online. You're a fake ****. You are.”Sneako then added another jab on X, writing: “Sorry, wish I could make the funeral but just can't miss the 24/7 AI n3on subathon stream.”For now, the feud appears to be about more than AI. It has exposed a deeper disagreement over how friends should handle criticism when their lives and careers play out in public.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Suspected smugglers on trial over deadliest migrant tragedy in France
articles.summary: Paris trial begins over deadly Channel tragedy, with 14 facing charges for manslaughter.
articles.body:
The trial for the accident involving at least 31 migrants and asylum seekers killed while trying to reach the United Kingdom has begun, with 14 men facing smuggling-related charges.

Some 114 civil parties, including victims’ families, are involved in the trial that opened on Tuesday. The incident was the deadliest disaster on record involving asylum seekers crossing the Channel separating France and the UK.

Twenty-seven people died after their inflatable dinghy deflated in one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes on November 24, 2021. Two men survived, and four others were left unaccounted for.

The victims were mostly Iraqi Kurds but also included nationals from Afghanistan, Ethiopia, Egypt, and Vietnam, aged between seven and 46.

Investigators say Afghan and Iraqi Kurdish migrant smuggling networks organised the crossing to the UK from camps in northern France.

The 14 defendants face charges including manslaughter and “facilitating illegal immigration as part of an organised gang”. Only nine suspects were present at the opening of the trial in a Parisian court, one of whom was in custody. The trial is expected to last three weeks.

Prosecutors accused the defendants of launching a “substandard small boat, uncertified, unfit for navigation on the open sea, overcrowded and lacking appropriate life jackets”.

Two of the suspects will be tried in absentia after eluding French authorities.

A French fishing vessel alerted authorities after reporting bodies floating in the Channel near the UK, according to a court document.

“Around 2:30am, we began bailing water out. But suddenly, the boat capsized,” survivor Issa Omar said in a statement read out in court.

A UK inquiry published in February found that some of the deaths were avoidable and concluded that a French naval vessel failed to respond to an alert from the UK coastguard.

Despite dozens of distress calls made to the UK and French rescue services, it was nearly 12 hours before the boat was finally found.

articles.title: US destroys five Iranian tankers, Iran retaliates with attacks on Jordan
articles.summary: US military says it struck the five Iranian tankers after IRGC targeted a US warship twice in two days.
articles.body:
The United States says it has destroyed five Iranian oil tankers in the Gulf after accusing Iran of launching ballistic missiles at a US warship twice in two days.

Iran responded to Tuesday’s attacks by firing missiles at US forces stationed at the Al Azraq base in Jordan. Amman said its air defences intercepted and destroyed 18 of 20 Iranian missiles, while the rest fell in open areas.

The exchange comes as tensions escalate between the two sides, with a standoff in the Strait of Hormuz intensifying six months after the US and Israel launched their war on Iran.

The hostilities briefly pushed oil prices to $99.46 earlier in the day.

The exchange of fire comes amid escalating tensions in the Gulf, six months into the US and Israel’s war on Iran, with Tehran closing the Strait of Hormuz and Washington imposing a naval blockade on Iranian ports.

The hostilities briefly drove oil prices to $99.46 earlier on Tuesday.

In a statement, the US Central Command said Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps had targeted a US warship twice over the past two days. The warship “successfully evaded the attempted Iranian attacks” and “no American personnel were harmed”, it said.

The Central Command said it retaliated by destroying the Iranian oil carriers, M/T Kaviz, M/T Charminar, M/T Horizon 1, and M/T Riesco in the Gulf of Oman as well as M/T Derya near Kharg Island.

“American forces directed the crews to abandon ship before the vessels were struck and rendered inoperable,” the Central Command added.

Iran’s IRIB state broadcaster confirmed the attack near Kharg Island in the Gulf, which handled some 90 percent of Iran’s oil exports before the war.

It reported that the crew was evacuated and said a second tanker was hit near the southern port of Jask on the Gulf of Oman.

The IRGC also said “several” Iranian commercial ships were hit, and said it retaliated by subjecting Al Azraq base in Jordan to “fierce missile strikes”. It claimed hangars used by US fighter jets were destroyed in the ballistic missile attacks.

It also threatened to target oil tankers in Kuwaiti and Bahraini ports, warning crews there to evacuate immediately.

Jordan’s Armed Forces, meanwhile, said its air defences engaged 20 ballistic missiles, “successfully intercepting and destroying 18 of them”. Two missiles “fell in unpopulated areas,” it said in a statement.

The attacks did not cause any casualties and specialised teams “have begun securing the locations where debris and shrapnel fell,” it added.

Earlier, the chief of staff of Iran’s Armed Forces, Ali Abdollahi, had warned that Tehran would strike US military installations across the region if Iranian tankers were targeted.

“The US aggressor army has given Iranian oil tankers an evacuation warning to hit them, so I announce that any attack on Iranian oil tankers will result in the targeting of US bases in the region by the armed forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran,” Abdollahi said on state TV.

articles.title: Marco Rubio says US seeks more economic and security ties in Latin America
articles.summary: The US secretary of state visits Colombia, Ecuador and Peru in a bid to enhance cooperation with right-wing allies.
articles.body:
United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said that the administration of President Donald Trump hopes to ink trade deals with Colombia, Peru and Ecuador soon, as the country seeks greater ties with right-wing allies across Latin America.

Rubio met with Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella during a visit to Barranquilla, Colombia, on Tuesday, part of a three-nation trip aimed at consolidating relations with allied governments and expanding US military involvement in the region.

“We have a lot of common interest with them, both taking on regional transnational criminal terrorism and also economic engagements,” Rubio said of the three countries before departing. “It’s part of a trend that you’re seeing in the Western Hemisphere of alignment with US and US interests.”

In addition to Colombia, the US secretary of state is set to travel later this week to Ecuador and Peru to meet with their respective presidents, Daniel Noboa and Keiko Fujimori.

Before his departure to Colombia, Rubio explained that the US was seeking “good, solid” trade deals in the near future with all three countries.

The diplomatic tour comes as the Trump administration seeks to check China’s growing influence in Latin America.

China, for example, inked a free-trade agreement with Peru in 2009 and has since become the South American country’s top trading partner, beating the US.

The Trump administration has also pushed for greater control over the entire Western Hemisphere, as part of a policy platform informally called the “Donroe Doctrine”.

Security has been a centrepiece of that effort. Since taking office for a second term, Trump has authorised lethal military actions in Venezuela, the eastern Pacific Ocean and the Caribbean Sea, which he touted as critical to combat drug trafficking.

De la Espriella took office in August promising a return to a militarised approach towards crime and armed groups, in line with Trump’s priorities.

He has also pledged to pursue closer relations with the US, after clashes between Trump and former President Gustavo Petro, Colombia’s first elected leftist leader.

“Colombia wants to re-establish itself as the United States’ primary partner in hemispheric security,” De la Espriella said after his meeting with Rubio, which included the signing of agreements on critical minerals and civil nuclear cooperation.

De la Espriella indicated he would seek US support for military operations, including through radar and drone technology.

A political newcomer with no prior experience in elected office, de la Espriella has been part of a wave of right-wing victories across Latin America in recent years.

The Trump administration has buttressed the electoral campaigns of the region’s conservative candidates by pledging financial and political support.

He has also invited them to join the “Shield of the Americas”, known as the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition (ACCC), a regional security framework that emphasises US military involvement to combat drugs and crime.

Leftist presidential candidate Ivan Cepeda, a Petro ally, slammed Rubio’s visit to Colombia as an “act of surrendering strategic aspects of our sovereignty”, pointing to Tuesday’s mineral and energy deals.

Cepeda also criticised de la Espriella’s decision to loosen gun restrictions on the same day, a position that echoes Trump administration policy.

“Just how disastrous the ‘memoranda of understanding’ that Rubio and De la Espriella are set to sign must be, given that an equally disastrous decision — the authorization to carry weapons — is being announced at the same time,” Cepeda wrote on social media.

Colombia has asked the Trump administration to lower tariffs imposed on the country in July.
